subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is a rapid, toxin‑mediated systemic illness caused by superantigens from Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes. Massive T‑cell activation leads to cytokine storm, hypotension, rash and multi‑organ failure.

sections.p: TSS is a medical emergency where bacterial superantigens trigger uncontrolled immune activation, causing fever, shock, rash and organ dysfunction within hours.
b: Incidence peaks in menstruating women using high‑absorbency tampons and in postoperative wound infections.
Mortality can exceed 30 % without prompt treatment.

sections.p: Most cases involve Staphylococcus aureus producing TSST‑1; Streptococcus pyogenes can cause a similar syndrome via streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins.
b: Gram‑positive cocci in clusters (S. aureus) or chains (S. pyogenes).
Superantigens bind directly to MHC‑II and the Vβ region of T‑cells, bypassing antigen specificity.

sections.p: The bacteria colonise skin, nares or mucosa; toxin production occurs when they proliferate in a protected niche such as a tampon, surgical wound or necrotic tissue.
b: No person‑to‑person spread of toxin; infection spreads by direct contact with colonised skin or contaminated devices.
Low‑resource settings: poor wound hygiene, prolonged catheter use, traditional herbal dressings.

sections.p: TSS presents with sudden high fever, diffuse erythematous rash (including palms/soles), hypotension, desquamation, and rapid organ failure (renal, hepatic, pulmonary).
b: Diagnostic criteria (CDC): fever ≥ 38.9 °C, rash, desquamation, hypotension, and ≥ 3 organ‑system involvement.
Staphylococcal TSS often follows tampon or postoperative wound; streptococcal TSS follows necrotising fasciitis or severe cellulitis.

sections.p: Clinical suspicion drives work‑up; laboratory tests confirm organ involvement and identify the pathogen when possible.
b: Blood cultures positive in < 30 % of cases; negative cultures do not exclude TSS.
Elevated liver enzymes, creatinine, and creatine kinase reflect organ injury.

t.b: Is a bacterial bloodstream infection present? Positive culture supports infection; negative does not rule out toxin‑mediated TSS.
Is there leukocytosis or left shift? High WBC supports systemic inflammation; low WBC may suggest overwhelming sepsis.
Is renal function impaired? Rising values indicate acute kidney injury, a key organ criterion.
Are transaminases elevated? Confirms hepatic involvement, part of the organ‑system count.
Is there coagulopathy? Low fibrinogen or prolonged PT suggests consumptive coagulopathy, worsening prognosis.

sections.p: Management combines rapid toxin‑source control, empiric antibiotics, and aggressive supportive care.
b: Remove tampon, drain abscess, or replace contaminated catheter immediately.
IV clindamycin suppresses toxin synthesis; combine with a β‑lactam (e.g., oxacillin) for bacterial kill.
Fluid resuscitation with crystalloids to maintain MAP > 65 mmHg; vasopressors if refractory.
Monitor urine output, liver enzymes, and coagulation; treat organ failure per ICU protocols.

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams and clinical reasoning.
b: TSS is a toxin‑mediated disease – antibiotics alone are insufficient without source control.
Clindamycin is essential because it blocks protein synthesis and toxin production.
Desquamation 1–2 weeks after rash is a classic clue distinguishing TSS from other rashes.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden fever with hypotension, rash, and rapid organ dysfunction
Progressive skin desquamation or severe abdominal pain

faq.q: Can a negative blood culture rule out TSS?
faq.a: No; toxin production can occur without bacteremia, so clinical criteria are paramount.

faq.q: Why is clindamycin preferred over other antibiotics?
faq.a: It inhibits bacterial protein synthesis, reducing superantigen production, unlike most β‑lactams.

faq.q: Is TSS only related to tampon use?
faq.a: No; non‑menstrual sources include surgical wounds, burns, and necrotising infections.

exam: List the CDC diagnostic criteria for toxic shock syndrome and explain why each organ system is included.
Describe the mechanism by which superantigens cause massive cytokine release.
Outline the immediate management steps for a patient with suspected TSS, including antimicrobial choice.
